source.title: The Statistical Model of Nuclear Reactions: Open Problems

accepted.question_text: In the statistical model of nuclear reactions, partial gamma decay widths for isolated neutron resonances are usually assumed to follow a Porter-Thomas distribution (PTD), and total gamma decay widths are then obtained by summing a very large number of such partial widths over many gamma decay channels. The paper asks whether replacing the PTD assumption for the partial gamma widths with a different distribution could produce a predicted distribution of total gamma decay widths for neutron resonances in the compound nucleus 96Mo that agrees better with the experimentally observed distribution, which is much broader and centered at larger values than the standard statistical-model prediction.

evidence.quote: That raises the question: Would a distribution of partial gamma widths different from the PTD yield better agreement of the predicted distribution of total gamma widths with the data of Ref. [3]?
However, Fig. 6 shows that use of the modified distribution for the gamma channels does not affect the disagreement with the data of Ref. [3].

accepted.question_text: The statistical model underpredicts the mean total gamma decay widths observed for neutron resonances and therefore appears to be missing gamma strength. The open question is whether the Brink-Axel hypothesis actually remains valid for all gamma transitions that contribute significantly to the gamma decay of those neutron resonances, since failure of that hypothesis could explain why the model does not reproduce the observed total gamma decay-width data.
accepted.context_brief: Brink-Axel validity for significant gamma transitions

evidence.quote: The small mean values of the total gamma decay widths predicted by the statistical model show that gamma strength is missing in the model. That poses the question whether the Brink-Axel hypothesis actually applies to all gamma transitions that contribute significantly to the gamma decay of the neutron resonances.

accepted.question_text: A possible way to reconcile the statistical model with the experimental total gamma decay-width data is that a comparatively small number of gamma transitions to low-lying final states are much more strongly coupled than the rest. Such channels would need to be intense enough to shift the simulated total gamma decay widths toward the experimental values and few enough in number to evade the central-limit-theorem narrowing that normally makes the predicted distribution too narrow. The open question is whether a comparatively small number of such strongly coupled gamma decay channels could also change the Porter-Thomas distribution behavior of the reduced neutron widths.
accepted.context_brief: Strong low-lying gamma channels and neutron-width PTD

evidence.quote: Given the experimental results, a small number of strong gamma transitions to low-lying final states might offer a way out of the dilemma [3]. These should have sufficient intensity to shift the simulated distribution of total gamma decay widths towards the experimental values. Their number should be sufficiently small to overcome the limits of the central-limit theorem and to broaden the distribution of total gamma decay widths.
It is an open question whether a comparatively small number of such strongly coupled gamma decay channels could also cause a change of the PTD for the reduced neutron widths.
